1.sense: The verb is passive, so something shakes the earth and the surah does not yet say what. Then the shaking is called hers, which separates it from every quake she has had before. This is the one that belongs to her.

notes.t: Zilzal is a doubled root, the shape Arabic uses for motion that repeats. The sound of the word is the thing it names, and the surah opens by making the reader say it.
Her shaking, with the possessive, is read as the quake appointed for her, the one she was always going to have. Every earthquake before it was a fragment of something; this is the whole of it.
The Qur'an names the quake of the Hour directly in another place and calls it an enormous thing, put at the very head of a surah as a warning.

links.why: the quake of the Hour named as the first thing in a surah
the earth convulsed at the same moment, told with a different verb

2.sense: Now the earth is the one acting. What she brings out is called her weights, the things she has been carrying all this time, and the word covers the dead in her ground and whatever else was put down into it.

notes.t: The verb is akhrajat, an active bringing out, not a losing or a spilling. The earth is described as handing something over rather than being emptied by force.
Thiql is a load. The Qur'an uses the same plural for the burdens that livestock carry to a distant town, which keeps the word in the register of freight rather than of horror.

Most exegetes read the burdens as the buried dead. Some include what else the ground holds, its metals and stores, and reports about the earth giving up its treasures near the end are discussed alongside this verse.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries the dead as the main reading and records the wider one

links.why: the earth casts out what is inside it and empties itself
when what is in the graves is turned out

3.sense: Two words of human speech are recorded, and they are a question. The entire response of the species to the end of the world is a puzzled phrase about the ground behaving oddly.

notes.t: Ma laha is low, ordinary spoken Arabic, the phrase used when a familiar thing starts acting strangely. The register is deliberate: no speech, no plea, just the noise a person makes when the floor moves.

Al-insan is definite and singular, the species standing there as one figure. The surah has three speakers in eight verses: man, the earth, and the Lord who instructed her, and this is the only one who does not know what is happening.
Some exegetes restrict the speaker to the denier, on the ground that a believer has been told what this is. Others leave it general, since shock is not a matter of creed.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the general reading and the restricted one

links.why: man will say that Day, where is the place to run
the eyes of those who denied fixed open at the sight of it

4.sense: The earth answers the question, and the answer is not an explanation of the quake. She reports what happened on her, which turns the ground under every act into the record of it.

notes.t: Haddatha is the plainest verb in Arabic for telling news, the root behind the word hadith. The ground is not giving evidence in a legal sense; it is talking, the way anyone talks about what they saw.

A report is transmitted that the Prophet ﷺ explained this verse as the earth testifying for or against each person about what was done on her surface. It comes through at-Tirmidhi and the chain is discussed by the critics.
notes.src: at-Tirmidhi reports it in his commentary on this surah and its chain is questioned

notes.t: The Qur'an already has skins, hands and feet speaking against their owners, so an earth that reports is inside a pattern rather than an exception to one.

links.why: they ask their own skins why they testified, and are answered
mouths sealed while hands speak and feet give evidence

5.sense: The reason the ground speaks is that it was told to. The verb is wahy, the same word used for what comes down to a prophet, and the earth is put on the receiving end of it.

notes.t: Awha in the Qur'an covers anything placed directly into a receiver: what is put to a bee about where to build, what is put to the mother of Musa about the basket, and what is put to a prophet. The word is about the channel, not the rank of the one receiving.

The usual Qur'anic construction is awha ila. Here it is awha laha, with a different preposition, and the exegetes note the change and read the lam as marking the earth's compliance rather than only the direction of the message.
notes.src: the commentators note the shift from ilā to the lām and explain it variously

notes.t: Rabbaka, your Lord, is the only second person address in the surah, and it is spoken to the Prophet ﷺ in the middle of a scene he is not in. The whole event is being narrated to one listener.

links.why: your Lord instructed the bee, the same verb for a creature under orders
He said to the sky and the earth, come willingly or unwillingly

6.sense: Sadara is the word for herds turning back from the water, the return leg after the crowding at the well. People come away in separate parties, and the reason given is not that they will be judged but that they will be shown.

notes.t: Sadara is the opposite of warada, going down to water. The Qur'an uses the pair at the well in Madyan, where Musa waits for the shepherds to draw off before he helps two women. The verse borrows a scene every desert listener had stood in.
Li-yuraw is passive: to be shown their deeds. They are not looking anything up. What they did is put in front of them by someone else, and the grammar gives them nothing to do but see.

Ashtat is scattered, separated into pieces that do not match. Everyone arrived at the same moment from the same ground and they leave it sorted, which is the first sign in the surah that the reckoning has already happened.

links.why: the same verb at a well, in its ordinary daily sense
they find everything they did present, and the record leaves nothing out

7.sense: The unit of measure is the smallest thing an Arab had a word for. And the verse does not say the deed is recorded or weighed or reported. It says the person sees it, which puts the act back in front of the eyes that once chose it.

notes.t: Dharra is explained by the lexicographers as the smallest ant, and also as the mote of dust you can only see in a shaft of light through a doorway. Either way it is chosen because it is the limit of what a person can notice.

The Prophet ﷺ was asked about donkeys and answered that nothing had come down to him about them except this one comprehensive verse, and then recited it. The report is well known and appears in more than one collection.
notes.src: Bukhari records it in the Book of Watering and again in his tafsir; also in Malik's Muwatta

notes.t: Mithqal is a weight, the same word used where the Qur'an describes the scales set up for the Day and says that even a mustard seed will be brought.

links.why: the just scales, down to the weight of a mustard seed
Allah does not wrong by so much as the weight of a speck

8.sense: The mirror of the verse before, changed by one word. The surah that opened with the whole planet coming apart closes on a quantity too small to be noticed, and both halves end with the same verb: he sees it.

notes.t: The two verses are identical except for khayran and sharran. Good is put first, and the Qur'an does that consistently when it pairs the two, so the reader meets the promise before the warning.
The surah moves from the largest event it can describe to the smallest act it can name, and joins them in eight verses. The quake exists so that the speck can be produced.
A report circulates that this surah equals half the Qur'an. It comes through at-Tirmidhi with a weak chain and the critics did not accept it, so it should not be repeated as the Prophet ﷺ's ﷺ words.
notes.src: at-Tirmidhi in the chapter on the merits of the Qur'an; the chain is weak and was not acted upon

links.why: the Day each self finds what it did of good present, and what it did of evil
a soul will know what it has put forward, at the end of a similar list
